title: Monks and Nuns
objective: After this level you can describe daily life in a monastery or convent.
summary: Monks and nuns lived by the Divine Office, eight services from matins in the night to compline, around a cloister; nuns lived the same pattern under abbesses in small, enclosed houses.

cards.headline: Imagine an alarm that goes off eight times a day, starting in the night.
cards.body: For medieval monks and nuns, that was simply the timetable. Level 7 gave you Benedict’s Rule. Now step inside the day it made.

cards.headline: The Divine Office
cards.body: The backbone of the day was the Divine Office: psalms, hymns, prayers and readings at set hours. Matins, the longest, came at night. Prime came early, lauds and vespers were the great morning and evening prayers, terce, sext and none marked mid-morning, noon and mid-afternoon, and compline was the night prayer. Remember Benedict’s balance of prayer, work and reading? The Office was the prayer. The work and study fitted in between.

cards.headline: A world around a square
cards.body: Life centered on the cloister, a square enclosure ringed by covered walkways. In a Benedictine house the church stood on one side and the refectory, the dining hall, faced it; the chapter house sat on the east and the dormitory upstairs. Young members were taught in the cloister and elders studied there. It was also for exercise, and its walks were where the dead were buried. School, gym and graveyard, all around one square.

cards.headline: Nuns and abbesses
cards.body: Women lived this life too. An abbess was the superior of a community of nuns following the Benedictine Rule, and some abbesses even ruled double monasteries of monks and nuns. An English nun’s day had the same three parts: eight services, devotional reading and manual labour. Strict enclosure kept nuns inside the walls, and most English houses were small: only a minority had more than a dozen or so nuns.

cards.headline: Monks and nuns: understood
learned: The Divine Office set eight services a day
The cloister joined church, refectory and dormitory
Abbesses led nuns under the Benedictine Rule
Most English nunneries were small and enclosed

questions.prompt: In a medieval monastery, what was the Divine Office?

options.label: The abbot’s room for running the house
options.rationale: It was a cycle of worship, not a room.

options.label: A tax that monks paid to the bishop
options.rationale: It was worship, not a payment.

options.label: Psalms, hymns and prayers sung at set hours
A yearly pilgrimage made by every monk

questions.explanation: The Divine Office was the daily cycle of psalms, hymns, prayers and readings, from matins in the night to compline.

questions.prompt: Why was the cloister the heart of a medieval monastery?

options.label: It linked church, refectory and dormitory, and hosted study
It was the only room where a fire was allowed
options.rationale: Its importance came from its layout and uses.

options.label: Travellers were received and fed there
options.rationale: It was the monks’ own space.

options.label: It held the monastery’s weekly market
options.rationale: It was for study, exercise and burial.

questions.explanation: The cloister joined the church, refectory, chapter house and dormitory, and it was where members studied, were taught, exercised and were buried.

questions.prompt: Level 7’s Benedict wrote his Rule for monks. How did it shape the lives of medieval nuns?

options.label: Nuns followed no written rule at all
Nuns could live only in double monasteries
options.rationale: Most lived in houses of nuns.

options.label: The Rule forbade nuns to read
options.rationale: Devotional reading was part of their day.

options.label: Abbesses led nuns under the same Rule

questions.explanation: An abbess was the superior of a community of nuns following the Benedictine Rule, and nuns’ days balanced services, reading and work.
